questions.q: What do metacognitive skills include?
options: Planning your learning, monitoring whether your strategies work and evaluating the results
questions.explain: Self-directed learners plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning.
questions.evidence: Metacognitive skills include planning your learning, monitoring whether your current learning strategies are successful, and evaluating results of your learning.

questions.q: In the learning cycle, which two tasks does planning involve?
options: Deciding what you need to learn and how you are going to learn it
Buying books and booking a room
Choosing a teacher and a course
Setting an exam date and a reward
questions.explain: Monitoring and evaluating follow planning in the cycle.
questions.evidence: Planning involves two key tasks: deciding what you need to learn, and then deciding how you are going to learn that material.

questions.q: What is a key element of self-efficacy?
questions.explain: Believing outcomes depend on your own actions supports persistence.
questions.evidence: A key element of self-efficacy is the concept of locus of control.

questions.q: What should you do when a goal feels too big to prepare for?
options: Give up and choose an easier goal
Develop smaller steps or tasks that you can start working on immediately
Wait until you have more time
Ask someone else to do it
questions.explain: Small, immediate steps beat waiting for the perfect moment.
questions.evidence: it’s important to develop smaller steps or tasks that can be started and worked on immediately.

questions.q: Why do we need goals?
options: Without goals we aren't sure what we're trying to accomplish or whether we are accomplishing anything
questions.explain: Goals give direction and a way to measure progress.
questions.evidence: Without goals, we aren’t sure what we are trying to accomplish, and there is little way of knowing if we are accomplishing anything.

questions.q: Which skill may you need to protect your study time from interruption?
questions.explain: Knowing when and where you concentrate best also helps.
questions.evidence: Saying “no” is an important skill that may need to be utilized in order for you to have your study time without interruption.

questions.q: What does the forgetting curve show?
options: That we never forget what we read
That sleep has no effect on memory
How much information is forgotten quickly after it is learned
questions.explain: Reviewing material soon after learning slows forgetting.
questions.evidence: known as the forgetting curve, shows how much information is forgotten quickly after it is learned.

questions.q: Why take good notes on what you read?
options: They help you quickly review the key points
Notes are required by every course
questions.explain: Note-taking makes you identify the important content and its implications.
questions.evidence: Taking good notes helps you to quickly review the key points in the material that you have read.

questions.q: Why are soft skills also called 'transferable skills'?
options: Because they are taught in transfer programmes
Because they expire when you change jobs
Because you can carry them from job to job or profession to profession without much training
Because employers transfer them to you
questions.explain: Communication, teamwork and problem-solving stay useful as technology changes.
questions.evidence: Soft skills are sometimes also called “transferable skills” because you can easily transfer them from job to job or profession to profession without much training.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what is the most effective way to find a new job?
options: To network, network and network some more
To send the same CV to every company
To wait for recruiters to call
To apply only through job boards
questions.explain: Relationships open doors that applications alone don't.
questions.evidence: the most effective way to find a new job is to network, network, and network some more.

questions.q: In a teacher-centred classroom, who decides what students learn?
options: The teacher, who directs the students
questions.explain: Self-directed learners take more of that responsibility themselves.
questions.evidence: In these classrooms, the teacher is the central figure, and the students take direction about what to learn directly from the instructor.

questions.q: Which model does the chapter suggest for assessing your own learning progress?
questions.explain: It is a practical way to use metacognition.
questions.evidence: Apply the Plan-Monitor-Evaluate Model for Assessing Your Learning Progress

questions.q: Which skill have students with effective ways of learning mastered?
questions.explain: Metacognition means thinking about how you think and learn.
questions.evidence: Students who have developed effective ways of learning have mastered a skill called metacognition.

questions.q: Where do some experts place 'world view' in how we think?
options: At the foundational level of how we think and perceive the world
questions.explain: World view shapes how we interpret everything else.
questions.evidence: world view, a concept some experts put at the foundational level of how we think and perceive the world

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does most of our time go on?
options: A mix of what interests us, what's important to us and what we feel we have to do
questions.explain: Time management is about balancing these.
questions.evidence: Most of us spend our time doing a combination of what interests us, what is important to us and what we feel we

questions.q: What do people often do once they realise how valuable their time is?
options: Go to great lengths to protect it
questions.explain: Valuing time is the first step to managing it.
questions.evidence: Once people realize how valuable time is, they often go to great lengths to protect it because they understand its importance.

questions.q: Since nobody can create more hours, what can we do?
options: Find better ways to spend our time
questions.explain: Better choices free time for the most important tasks and people.
questions.evidence: What we can do though, is find better ways to spend our time

questions.q: Why are long-term goals harder than short-term ones?
options: They are harder to create and harder to stay accountable to
questions.explain: Breaking them into smaller steps helps.
questions.evidence: Long-term goals are more difficult to create and it is more challenging for us to stay accountable.

questions.q: What separates a wish from a goal?
options: A wish has only a slim chance of happening
A goal is always about money
questions.explain: Goals should be realistic and achievable.
questions.evidence: a student might say that owning a Ferrari or becoming a movie star were wishes, not goals, because the chance of them happening is slim

questions.q: How does the chapter describe procrastination?
options: Doing a low-priority task instead of a high-priority one
questions.explain: It is about priorities, not just laziness.
questions.evidence: It’s doing something that’s a low priority instead of doing something that is a high priority.

questions.q: Why do some students struggle with time management at college?
options: College has less structure than high school
questions.explain: More freedom means more self-management.
questions.evidence: Other students may struggle because college does not have as much structure as what they may have been used to in high school.

questions.q: When we cannot 'do it all', what should we do?
options: Prioritise, let something go and re-evaluate what matters most
questions.explain: Adjusting priorities is part of realistic time management.
questions.evidence: Sometimes we need to prioritize, let something go, adjust and reevaluate what the most important things are to us.

questions.q: What does the chapter suggest about the causes of procrastination?
options: There may be more to it than laziness or disorganisation
questions.explain: Understanding the real cause is the first step to fixing it.
questions.evidence: Perhaps there is, in fact, more to your challenges with procrastination than the assumptions about laziness, disorganization, etc.

questions.q: Why follow the syllabus during lectures?
options: Because exams are on the syllabus only
To be familiar with what the instructor is talking about
questions.explain: Preparation makes lectures easier to follow.
questions.evidence: Follow the syllabus so that you’ll have familiarity with what the instructor is speaking about.

questions.q: Why take notes while you read?
options: To avoid reading the whole text
questions.explain: Writing helps move information into memory.
questions.evidence: it is helpful to take notes while you are reading to maximize memorization

questions.q: What should students check regularly to keep up with a course?
options: Email and the instructor's announcements in the learning platform
questions.explain: Important changes are often posted there first.
questions.evidence: It is important for students to check their e-mail regularly as well as Announcements or notifications from their instructor through the LMS.

questions.q: Once you have identified important information, what helps you understand it best?
options: Organising it in a way that suits you
questions.explain: Organised information is easier to store and retrieve.
questions.evidence: Once the important information is identified, it is helpful to organize it in a way that will help you best understand.

questions.q: Which skills do general education courses often develop?
options: Only skills for one specific job
questions.explain: These skills are valuable in any career.
questions.evidence: skills like critical thinking, communication (both oral and written), and literacy are often developed from these courses

questions.q: What is Hypothesis?
options: A free browser tool for highlighting and annotating online text
questions.explain: Annotating as you read keeps your notes next to the source.
questions.evidence: Hypothesis is a free tool that you add to the Chrome browse that allows you to highlight and add notes to online text.

questions.q: What are hard skills?
options: Skills you can easily quantify, like using a computer or a foreign language
Skills that are hard to learn
questions.explain: Soft skills, by contrast, are transferable people skills.
questions.evidence: They are skills you can easily quantify, like using a computer, speaking a foreign language, or operating a machine.

questions.q: Why are the hard skills industries need today so different from centuries ago?
questions.explain: Soft skills, in contrast, have changed little.
questions.evidence: because of changes in technology, the hard skills required by industries today are vastly different from those required centuries ago

questions.q: How many main stages of career development did Donald Super describe?
questions.explain: They run from growing in childhood to later life stages.
questions.evidence: There are five main stages of career development (developed by Donald Super).

questions.q: What happens in the 'growing' stage of Super's model?
options: In early years (4–13) you begin to sense your future
questions.explain: Early interests often hint at later career choices.
questions.evidence: This is a time in early years (4–13 years old) when you begin to have a sense about the future.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say to master LinkedIn?
options: It is the only job site
questions.explain: Networking is the most effective way to find a new job.
questions.evidence: Master Linkedin because that is what human resource departments use.

questions.q: Why is volunteering good for your career, even outside your field?
options: It is an excellent way to meet people who can help your career
It always leads to a paid job there
questions.explain: Your network grows wherever you meet people.
questions.evidence: Volunteering is an excellent way to meet new people who can help you develop your career, even if the organization you are volunteering with is not in your field.
